title: Lipase, Amylase and Acute Liver Failure: Reading the Emergency Enzymes
summary: Learn why lipase is preferred over amylase in suspected acute pancreatitis yet is not definitive, why a normal amylase does not exclude pancreatitis, and why acute liver failure is defined by INR and encephalopathy rather than by the height of the AST.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 9 Hit 12 (lipase > amylase for pancreatitis; salivary amylase confounds), Trap 3 (a normal amylase does not exclude pancreatitis) and Hit 13 (fulminant hepatic failure). Checked against the WSES 2019 guideline, the Korean 2023 guideline, the Rompianesi 2017 Cochrane review (read via a page-fetch tool), Fernández 2024, Ozturk 2023 and Kalas 2021. Qualifications: Trap 3 calls lipase the “definitive, specific” marker, while the Cochrane review found similar specificity for both enzymes (lipase 0.89, amylase 0.93) with lipase preferred for sensitivity and diagnostic window, and about a quarter of cases missed (register flag rv-lipase-definitive-ch9). Hit 13 characterizes fulminant hepatic failure by AST > 10,000 IU/L with AST > ALT and low albumin; the sources define acute liver failure by INR ≥ 1.5 plus encephalopathy without pre-existing liver disease, and aminotransferase height varies by cause (register flag rv-alf-enzyme-definition-ch9). Not taught: the hemolysis panel in Hit 12 (haptoglobin, indirect bilirubin, LD, potassium, reticulocytes), low albumin in acute liver failure, and the Number Vault ammonia upper limit (30 µmol/L), which no source read here supports.

objectives: Explain why serum amylase is less useful than lipase and why a normal amylase does not exclude acute pancreatitis.
Apply the two-of-three criteria and state the sensitivity and specificity limits of both enzymes.
Define acute liver failure by INR and encephalopathy, and interpret aminotransferase height, falling aminotransferases and ammonia.

scenes.title: Two emergencies, two misleading numbers
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: two emergency-room adults. (A) Epigastric pain radiating to the back for 6 days; serum amylase within the reference interval; lipase 5 times the upper limit of normal. (B) Three days after a paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose, no known liver disease: AST 9,800 U/L, ALT 8,600 U/L, INR 3.4, newly confused. Question token: “Pancreatitis excluded? Liver failure because of the AST?”

cues.text: Patient A has had pain in the upper abdomen, boring into the back, for six days. The amylase is normal, but the lipase is five times the upper limit.
Patient B took a paracetamol overdose three days ago. Aminotransferases are near ten thousand, the INR is three point four, and she is newly confused.
Does the normal amylase exclude pancreatitis? And is it the huge AST that makes this liver failure?

props.label: Pancreatitis excluded? Liver failure because of the AST?

scenes.title: Two pancreatic enzymes, two clocks
scenes.altText: Schematic enzyme cards. Amylase is made by the pancreas and also by the salivary glands, small intestine, ovaries, adipose tissue and skeletal muscle; the pancreas supplies only about 40% of total serum amylase, most of the rest coming from salivary glands. Lipase is secreted by the pancreas. Timing in acute pancreatitis (WSES 2019): amylase rises within 6–24 h, peaks about 48 h, and returns to normal or near normal over 3–7 days; lipase rises within 4–8 h, peaks about 24 h, and returns to normal or near normal over 8–14 days.

cues.text: Amylase is not only a pancreatic enzyme. Salivary glands, gut, ovaries, fat and muscle make it too, and the pancreas supplies only about forty percent of serum amylase.
Lipase is secreted by the pancreas, and acute pancreatitis is the main reason it rises.
The clocks differ. Amylase rises within six to twenty-four hours, peaks around two days, and is back to normal or near normal within three to seven days.
Lipase rises within four to eight hours, peaks around one day, and stays raised for eight to fourteen days. So a late presenter can have a normal amylase while the lipase is still raised.

props.title: Lipase
lines: Acute pancreatitis: main cause of rise

scenes.title: Why lipase is preferred, and why it is not definitive
scenes.altText: Criteria card: acute pancreatitis is diagnosed with at least two of three — typical abdominal pain; serum amylase and/or lipase at least three times the upper limit of normal; characteristic imaging. Accuracy card (Cochrane review, Rompianesi 2017, at >3 × ULN): serum amylase sensitivity 0.72, specificity 0.93; serum lipase sensitivity 0.79, specificity 0.89; about a quarter of people with acute pancreatitis are missed by these tests. Preference card: most guidelines prefer lipase, mainly for higher sensitivity and a longer diagnostic window. Caution card: lipase can also rise in renal disease, appendicitis, acute cholecystitis, chronic pancreatitis and bowel obstruction.

cues.text: Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed with two of three criteria: typical pain, amylase or lipase at least three times the upper limit, and typical imaging. An enzyme alone is one criterion, not the diagnosis.

In a Cochrane review at three times the upper limit, amylase had a sensitivity of about seventy-two percent, and lipase about seventy-nine percent. Specificity was similar, about ninety-three and eighty-nine percent.

So guidelines prefer lipase mainly because it catches more cases and stays raised longer, not because it is perfectly specific. About a quarter of patients with pancreatitis are still missed by these tests.
Lipase can also rise outside acute pancreatitis: in renal disease, appendicitis, cholecystitis, chronic pancreatitis and bowel obstruction.

props.label: Lipase preferred: more sensitive, longer window · ~¼ still missed
Lipase also ↑: renal disease, appendicitis, cholecystitis, obstruction

scenes.title: Acute liver failure is defined by function, not enzymes
scenes.altText: Definition card: acute liver failure = INR of 1.5 or more plus hepatic encephalopathy in a patient without pre-existing liver disease, with illness under 26 weeks (AASLD/ACG, as summarized by Ozturk 2023); INR above 1.5 without encephalopathy (with marked liver injury) = acute liver injury. Aminotransferase card (Ozturk 2023 table): paracetamol often above 3,500 IU/L; ischemic injury very high; hepatitis B 1,000–2,000; acute fatty liver of pregnancy under 1,000. Falling aminotransferases with rising bilirubin and INR are a poor sign. Ammonia card: the failing liver cannot convert ammonia to urea; serum ammonia of 150–200 µmol/L is associated with higher risk of cerebral edema. Hook answers: A = acute pancreatitis (pain + lipase ≥3 × ULN); B = acute liver failure because of INR ≥1.5 plus encephalopathy, not because of the AST value; urgent transfer to a transplant centre.

cues.text: Acute liver failure is defined by function: an INR of one point five or more plus hepatic encephalopathy, in someone without previous liver disease, within twenty-six weeks. A high INR without encephalopathy is called acute liver injury.

Aminotransferase height depends on the cause: often above three thousand five hundred after paracetamol, very high in ischemic injury, about one to two thousand in hepatitis B, and under one thousand in fatty liver of pregnancy. And falling enzymes with rising bilirubin and INR are a bad sign, not recovery.
The failing liver cannot turn ammonia into urea. A high ammonia, around one hundred fifty to two hundred micromoles per litre, is linked to a higher risk of brain swelling.

Back to the hook. Patient A meets two criteria, pain and lipase, so pancreatitis is likely despite the normal amylase. Patient B has acute liver failure because of the INR and the confusion, not the AST, and needs urgent transfer to a transplant centre.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A normal amylase excludes pancreatitis” (✓ amylase normalizes within 3–7 days and misses cases; check lipase and the two-of-three criteria); “Lipase is the definitive test” (✓ preferred for sensitivity and window, but about a quarter of cases are missed and lipase rises in other diseases); “AST above 10,000 defines fulminant liver failure” (✓ INR ≥1.5 plus encephalopathy defines it; enzyme height varies by cause).

cues.text: Trap one: a normal amylase excludes pancreatitis. No: amylase falls back within days and misses cases. Check lipase and the two-of-three criteria.
Trap two: lipase is the definitive test. No: it is preferred, but it misses some cases and rises in other diseases. It is one criterion of three.
Trap three: an AST above ten thousand defines liver failure. No: INR and encephalopathy define it, and enzyme height depends on the cause.

scenes.title: Lipase lingers; the liver is judged by clock and mind
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Amylase leaves early and leaks from the mouth; lipase lingers. A failing liver is judged by the clotting clock (INR) and the mind (encephalopathy), not by the enzyme meter.” Tokens: amylase = early exit, salivary leak · lipase = lingers 8–14 days · liver failure = INR + mind. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: amylase leaves early and leaks from the mouth; lipase lingers. A failing liver is judged by the clotting clock and the mind, the INR and encephalopathy, not by the enzyme meter.

Where it breaks: lipase also rises outside the pancreas, and about a quarter of pancreatitis cases are missed by both enzymes; the enzyme meter still helps point to the cause of liver failure; and a falling meter can mean the liver is running out of cells.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Pancreatitis: lipase preferred · 2 of 3 criteria · normal amylase ≠ excluded”, “Acute liver failure: INR ≥ 1.5 + encephalopathy · not the AST value”.

cues.text: Use lipase rather than amylase in suspected acute pancreatitis but read it as one of three criteria, and define acute liver failure by a raised INR with encephalopathy rather than by how high the aminotransferases climb.

props.label: Pancreatitis: lipase preferred · 2 of 3 criteria · normal amylase ≠ excluded
Acute liver failure: INR ≥ 1.5 + encephalopathy · not the AST value

explanation.what: Plain language: in pancreatitis, the amylase level can be normal by the time the patient arrives and can come from the salivary glands, so lipase is the better enzyme, but neither enzyme alone makes the diagnosis. In acute liver failure, liver function fails, so the INR rises and ammonia is not cleared; what defines it is a raised INR and confusion, not how high the liver enzymes go. Scientific terms: serum amylase (pancreatic and salivary isoforms), serum lipase, upper limit of normal (ULN), revised Atlanta-type two-of-three criteria, acute liver failure (ALF), acute liver injury (ALI), hepatic encephalopathy (HE), international normalized ratio (INR), aminotransferases (AST, ALT), arterial ammonia, King’s College criteria.
explanation.why: Amylase is made by many tissues and clears within days, so it can be normal late or raised for non-pancreatic reasons. Lipase rises sooner and stays up longer (8–14 days), which gives it a wider diagnostic window and higher sensitivity. In acute liver failure the INR rises as liver function fails, and the failing liver cannot convert ammonia to urea; ammonia contributes to astrocyte swelling and cerebral edema. Aminotransferase height varies with the cause of injury, and the values can fall as liver cell mass is lost.
explanation.measure: Pancreatitis: two of three criteria (pain; amylase and/or lipase ≥ 3 × ULN; imaging). Amylase rises 6–24 h, peaks ~48 h, normal by 3–7 days; lipase rises 4–8 h, peaks ~24 h, normal by 8–14 days. Cochrane (> 3 × ULN): amylase sensitivity 0.72, specificity 0.93; lipase sensitivity 0.79, specificity 0.89. Acute liver failure: INR ≥ 1.5 + HE, no pre-existing liver disease, < 26 weeks; ALI = INR > 1.5 without HE. Paracetamol injury often > 3,500 IU/L; HBV 1,000–2,000; acute fatty liver of pregnancy < 1,000. Ammonia around 150–200 µmol/L = higher cerebral-edema risk. King’s College criteria (paracetamol): arterial pH < 7.3 after resuscitation, or HE grade ≥ 3 + creatinine > 300 µmol/L + INR > 6.5.
explanation.differs: Amylase (many tissues, short window) vs lipase (pancreas, longer window, higher point-estimate sensitivity, not more specific; the Cochrane review could not compare them formally); acute liver injury (INR > 1.5, no encephalopathy) vs acute liver failure (INR ≥ 1.5 with encephalopathy); acute liver failure vs acute-on-chronic liver failure (pre-existing disease).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: choose lipase for a late presenter with a normal amylase, apply the two-of-three rule, recognise that enzyme levels do not define liver failure, and interpret falling aminotransferases with rising INR and bilirubin as worsening.

Enzyme and liver cards are schematic.
Accuracy figures come from one Cochrane review with wide confidence intervals; assays and reference limits differ.
takeaway: Use lipase rather than amylase in suspected acute pancreatitis but read it as one of three criteria, and define acute liver failure by a raised INR with encephalopathy rather than by how high the aminotransferases climb.

questions.stem: On day 6 of epigastric pain radiating to the back, a patient’s serum amylase is within the reference interval and the lipase is 5 times the upper limit of normal. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Acute pancreatitis is likely: pain plus lipase ≥ 3 × ULN meets two of three criteria, and amylase can normalize within 3–7 days
options.rationale: Correct. Lipase stays raised for 8–14 days, so it can still be raised in a late presenter after amylase has normalized.

options.text: Pancreatitis is excluded because the amylase is normal
options.rationale: Incorrect. Amylase clears within days and misses cases; a normal value does not exclude pancreatitis.

options.text: The raised lipase alone proves pancreatitis, so imaging is never needed
options.rationale: Incorrect. Lipase is one criterion; it can rise in other diseases, and characteristic imaging is one of the three diagnostic criteria.

options.text: Salivary gland disease is the most likely source
options.rationale: Incorrect. Salivary glands are a source of amylase, and the amylase here is normal; lipase is a pancreatic enzyme, and pain plus lipase at least 3 × ULN meet two criteria for pancreatitis.

questions.stem: Which finding defines acute liver failure in a patient with no previous liver disease?

options.text: INR of 1.5 or more together with hepatic encephalopathy
options.rationale: Correct. Both coagulopathy and encephalopathy are required, within 26 weeks of illness onset.
Incorrect. Aminotransferase height varies by cause and is not part of the definition.
Incorrect. Coagulopathy without encephalopathy is acute liver injury, which precedes most cases of acute liver failure but is not failure itself.
Incorrect. The ratio may hint at a cause but does not define liver failure.

questions.stem: In a patient with acute liver failure, ALT falls from 8,000 to 1,500 U/L over 3 days while bilirubin and INR keep rising. What does this pattern most likely mean?

options.text: Worsening failure with loss of hepatocyte mass; a poor prognostic sign needing a transplant centre
options.rationale: Correct. Falling aminotransferases with rising bilirubin and INR are a poor sign.

options.text: Recovery, because the aminotransferases are falling
options.rationale: Incorrect. Falling aminotransferases may reflect recovery, but with rising INR and bilirubin they are a poor prognostic sign.

options.text: A laboratory error in the ALT assay
options.rationale: Incorrect. The pattern is clinically recognized and should not be dismissed as error.
Incorrect. Nothing here points to chronic disease; the rising INR and bilirubin show worsening acute failure.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 9 Trap 3 (and Memory Hook “Lipase leads; amylase misleads”) calls lipase the definitive, specific marker for pancreatitis. The Rompianesi 2017 Cochrane review found lipase sensitivity 0.79 and specificity 0.89 versus amylase 0.72 and 0.93, with about a quarter of cases missed; WSES 2019 prefers lipase mainly for higher sensitivity and a longer diagnostic window and notes non-pancreatic causes of raised lipase. The lesson teaches lipase as preferred but as one of two-of-three criteria (register flag rv-lipase-definitive-ch9).

Ch. 9 Hit 13 describes fulminant hepatic failure by AST often > 10,000 IU/L with AST > ALT, low albumin/protein and high ammonia. Ozturk 2023 and Fernández 2024 define acute liver failure by INR ≥ 1.5 plus hepatic encephalopathy without pre-existing liver disease; aminotransferase height varies widely by cause (often < 1,000–2,000 in hepatitis B or acute fatty liver of pregnancy), and falling aminotransferases can mean worsening. Low albumin was not found as a feature in the sources read. The lesson teaches the function-based definition (register flag rv-alf-enzyme-definition-ch9).
